title: Hair Fall (Khalitya): Ayurvedic Causes, Diet & Hair Care
excerpt: A bunch of hair in the comb, hair on the pillow, a thinning plait — hair fall is a very common worry today. Learn how much hair fall is normal, the causes from the Ayurvedic view, the tests needed, what to eat and what to avoid, correct hair care, safe home remedies, and when you must see a doctor immediately.
content:
“As soon as I comb, a bunch of hair comes out” — this complaint is heard today from men and women of every age. Hair fall is not only about looks; sometimes it is the first sign of a deficiency or imbalance inside the body — such as low blood (anaemia), thyroid or hormonal problems.

The good news is that in most cases, by identifying the right cause, with a balanced diet, good sleep, less stress and correct hair care, hair fall can be reduced a great deal. This article is for information only — take treatment only on the advice of your Vaidya or doctor.

How much hair fall is normal?

Hair falling and new hair growing is a natural cycle. Normally, losing about 50 to 100 hairs a day is common, and new hair keeps growing in their place. You should be concerned when:

  • Much more hair than usual falls daily and this continues for several weeks
  • The parting widens, the plait becomes thin or the scalp starts showing
  • Hair starts receding from the sides of the forehead or from the top of the head
  • Round smooth bald patches appear on the scalp

The Ayurvedic view

In Ayurveda, hair fall is called Khalitya, and loss of hair in patches is called Indralupta. Hair is considered the mala (by-product) of Asthi dhatu, so good digestion, nutrition and balanced dhatus are needed for good hair. Acharya Sushruta has described its cause as follows:

रोमकूपानुगं पित्तं वातेन सह मूर्च्छितम् ।
प्रच्यावयति रोमाणि ततः श्लेष्मा सशोणितः ॥
— Sushruta Samhita, Nidana Sthana 13

Meaning: Pitta that has reached the hair roots (romakupa), combining with Vata, makes the hair fall; then Kapha together with Rakta (blood) blocks those hair roots, so that new hair cannot grow easily.

That is why very spicy-sour-salty food, anger, stress, sun and heat, and staying up late — which increase Pitta and Vata — are considered enemies of hair. The basis of care in Ayurveda is — calming Pitta and Vata, keeping Agni and nutrition right, and keeping the scalp clean and nourished with oil.

Main causes

  • Hereditary (pattern) baldness — in men from the forehead and top of the head, in women thinning near the parting
  • Sudden heavy shedding (telogen effluvium) — about 2–3 months after high fever, an illness like dengue, typhoid or COVID, surgery, childbirth, a severe emotional shock or rapid weight loss
  • Nutritional deficiency — iron (anaemia), protein, vitamin B12, vitamin D and zinc
  • Low or high thyroid, hormonal problems like PCOS, menopause
  • Scalp diseases — dandruff, psoriasis, fungal infection
  • Alopecia areata — hair loss in round patches due to a disturbance of the immune system
  • Tight plaits or buns, frequent hair dye, straightening, bleach and very hot dryers
  • Some medicines and treatments — such as cancer chemotherapy, some blood thinners; long-term stress and lack of sleep

Tests

The cause of hair fall differs from person to person, so changing oils and shampoos without knowing the cause often does not help. The doctor or Vaidya looks at the hair and scalp, asks about your diet, illnesses and medicines, and may order these tests as needed:

  • CBC and ferritin — to detect low blood and iron deficiency
  • TSH — thyroid test
  • Vitamin B12 and vitamin D
  • In women with irregular periods, acne or excess facial hair — hormone tests (for PCOS)

Diet: what to eat, what to avoid

Hair is made of protein and needs iron, vitamins and minerals. According to Ayurveda, food should keep Pitta calm and nourish the dhatus.

What to eat

  • Protein in every meal — dals, chana, rajma, moong, paneer, milk-curd; eggs and fish if you are non-vegetarian
  • For iron — green leafy vegetables (spinach, fenugreek, bathua), jaggery-chana, pomegranate; along with vitamin C fruits like amla, guava, orange
  • Amla — considered the best for hair and as a rasayana in Ayurveda; fresh in season or as murabba (avoid murabba in diabetes)
  • Soaked almonds, walnuts, flaxseed, pumpkin and sesame seeds
  • A little desi ghee in food; seasonal fruits and vegetables
  • Enough water and coconut water

What to avoid

  • Very spicy, sour, salty and oily-fried food — these increase Pitta
  • Too much sugar, maida, junk food and cold drinks
  • Smoking, alcohol and too much tea-coffee
  • Crash dieting — losing weight fast by eating very little

Do not take iron, biotin or other supplements on your own for long periods without tests — excess of some also causes harm, and biotin can disturb the reports of some blood tests (such as thyroid).

Daily routine and hair care

In Ayurveda, Shiro-abhyanga (oiling the head) is described as part of the daily routine. Some simple habits for hair:

  • Gentle massage with the fingertips using lukewarm oil (like coconut or sesame oil) 2–3 times a week, then wash the hair after a few hours
  • Keep the scalp clean with a mild shampoo; do not wash the head with very hot water
  • Do not comb wet hair, use a wide-toothed comb; do not tie hair tightly
  • Keep hair dye, straightening and hot dryers to a minimum; cover the head in the sun
  • 7–8 hours of sleep daily; reduce staying up late and using the mobile late at night

Yoga and pranayama

Stress is a big cause of hair fall. Anulom-Vilom, Bhramari, Sheetali pranayama and meditation are considered helpful in reducing stress; Vajrasana and Balasana can also be done. Caution: in high blood pressure, glaucoma or pregnancy, do not do head-down poses (like Shirshasana, Adho Mukha Svanasana) without asking your doctor. Learn yoga from a trained teacher.

Safe home remedies

  • Amla: fresh amla or amla powder as part of food
  • Fenugreek seeds: soak at night, grind, apply as a paste on the scalp and wash off after about half an hour
  • Curd or aloe vera gel: apply on the scalp in dandruff and dryness, then wash off
  • Lukewarm coconut oil: gentle massage — do not rub very hard

Test any new paste first on a small area behind the ear; do not apply if there is burning or itching. Applying onion or lemon juice directly on the scalp can cause irritation in some people.

Ayurvedic herbs — with caution

Ayurveda mentions several medicines for hair, such as — Bhringraj, Amla, Brahmi, Yashtimadhu (mulethi), Ashwagandha and classical oils like Nilibhringadi taila. For Khalitya, Nasya karma (a procedure of putting medicated oil in the nose) under a Vaidya's supervision is also specially mentioned. However:

  • Which medicine, in what dose and for how long — the Vaidya decides this only after looking at each person's prakriti, pulse, age, the cause of hair fall and current medicines.
  • Do not stop your current medicines for thyroid, PCOS or skin disease on your own — Ayurvedic treatment can run alongside, but only the doctor should change the medicine.
  • Some herbs like Ashwagandha can change thyroid levels; taking Yashtimadhu (mulethi) for a long time can raise BP — so do not take them without advice.
  • In pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and the elderly, give any medicine only on the advice of a Vaidya/doctor. Beware of claims like “sure cure for baldness” or “new hair in one week”.

When to see a doctor immediately

  • Hair suddenly falling in clumps, or round smooth patches appearing on the scalp
  • Hair fall with pain, redness, scaling, pus or sores on the scalp
  • Hair also falling from the eyebrows, eyelashes or other parts of the body
  • Hair fall with great tiredness, change in weight, feeling too cold or too hot, or a fast heartbeat
  • In women, hair fall with irregular periods, acne or excess facial hair
  • Hair fall in children, or hair fall after starting a new medicine (do not stop the medicine on your own, ask your doctor)

Summary — points to remember

  • Losing 50–100 hairs a day is normal; if more, find the cause
  • Get blood, iron, thyroid and vitamin tests done
  • Protein- and iron-rich diet, amla; less spicy-fried and junk food
  • Good sleep, less stress, gentle oil massage of the scalp; fewer chemical treatments
  • Medicines only on the advice of an experienced Vaidya; if hair falls in patches, see a doctor immediately
